claims.text: OAuth 2.0 defines four roles: resource owner, client, authorization server (issues access tokens after authenticating the resource owner) and resource server (serves protected resources to requests that carry access tokens).

With OAuth 2.0 a client obtains an access token instead of using the resource owner's credentials, so it need not hold the password; in Đơn Hàng it never does (donhang-app directAccessGrantsEnabled: false).
claims.source_hint: RFC 6749 §1 Introduction, §1.3.3 (password grant exists but is disabled here); keycloak/donhang-realm.json@stage-2:24

claims.text: Đơn Hàng stage-2 mapping: customer = resource owner, DonHang.App = client registered as clientId donhang-app in keycloak/donhang-realm.json, Keycloak = authorization server, DonHang.Api = resource server.
At stage-2 DonHang.App's login screen has no password field: signing in sends the browser to Keycloak's login page, published at localhost:8180, where the customer types email and password.

At stage-1, DonHang.App sent email and password to POST /api/v1/auth/login, where AuthController checked them with PasswordHasher.Verify against customers.password_hash and returned a JwtTokenService token.

Stage-2 removed POST /api/v1/auth/login, AuthController, JwtTokenService and PasswordHasher, and dropped customers.password_hash with the migration DropCustomerPasswordHash; the accounts and their passwords live in the Keycloak realm (users[].credentials).
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-2: STAGE.md 'Changed since stage-1'; DonHang.Infrastructure/Migrations/20260927110119_DropCustomerPasswordHash.cs; keycloak/donhang-realm.json:63-130

claims.text: The client sends the access token in the Authorization header as the word Bearer, a space, then the token, as DonHang.App and the scripts did with the stage-1 token (auth-and-orders.sh: -H "Authorization: Bearer $token").
claims.source_hint: RFC 6749 §7.1 Access Token Types (bearer); examples/don-hang @ stage-2: scripts/backend/auth-and-orders.sh; DonHang.App/lib/api_client.dart

claims.text: Program.cs reads Keycloak:Authority from configuration, throws InvalidOperationException at startup when it is missing, and sets JwtBearerOptions.Authority to it; the api no longer holds a signing key.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-2: DonHang.Api/Program.cs:40-45; ASP.NET Core docs: JwtBearerOptions.Authority

claims.text: The API still validates the token on requests to [Authorize] endpoints; without a valid token they get 401 (POST /api/v1/orders in auth-and-orders.sh). GET /api/v1/products has no [Authorize] and answers without a token.
Keycloak start-dev keeps its data inside the container, and --import-realm imports the realm file from /opt/keycloak/data/import at startup (the first time, when the realm does not exist yet).
claims.source_hint: Keycloak docs: Importing and exporting realms (--import-realm); Configuring Keycloak for development (start-dev, dev-file database)

claims.text: auth-and-orders.sh signs in customer 1 at Keycloak (password only in that step), places an order with the token, reads it back, then POSTs without a token: output shows 'got a token: eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...', customerId 1 twice, last line 401.
Keeping the password in one place (the authorization server) means a bug, log or copy of the app or the API cannot leak it, because they never hold it.
claims.source_hint: reasoning from RFC 6749 §1 and the stage-2 design; no official number

claims.text: A Keycloak realm is a separate set of users, roles and registered clients; the Đơn Hàng realm is 'donhang', and Keycloak issues tokens only to clients registered in the realm.
claims.source_hint: Keycloak Server Administration Guide: Core concepts and terms (realm, client); keycloak/donhang-realm.json@stage-2
